claims.claim: The strategy commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children 'will not be implemented' and teardown stays a manual one-at-a-time operator action, while the PRD schedules exactly that feature: a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) on ApplicationSetStrategy that automates ordered deletion of generated Applications. Both commitments cannot hold; note-2 flags the disagreement as needing an owner but records none.

RFC-001 states as a goal that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' and applies to all Applications once flipped, but the platform sync decided rollout goes 'behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide', and T-26271 reports the flag already enabled per-project in production ('projects where we recently enabled the sync impersonation flag'). The rollout mechanism in use is one the approved design says does not exist.

RFC-002's goal 4 requires that 'every deployed change must have a corresponding dry commit', but the rollback design in T-27327 deploys by checking out old rendered manifests directly onto the sync branch, bypassing the staging branch and any dry commit. The rollback plan violates the hydrator's core invariant, and per note-1 the pair that would reconcile this was moved off the rollback ticket to the deletion loop.

T-26271's CI diff failures were root-caused at the platform sync: with impersonation on, the diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources; the reporter is still chasing the broad cluster Secret credential because the root cause was never written onto the ticket. T-28695 is the same mechanism surfacing on the application-controller path for external clusters, where Server-Side Diff's dry-run apply requires unbounded patch RBAC.

The interim restriction that 'nobody flips [impersonation] on a project until the diff story is fixed' silently blocks more than the diff tickets: T-27833's requested namespace-security fix is proposed on top of the impersonation feature, and T-28695 warns that making Server-Side Diff the default (#24134) before diff honors destinationServiceAccounts breaks every external-cluster user on upgrade. Neither plan acknowledges the freeze.

The incident review's interim rule that 'hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce' forbids the exact configuration T-27949 describes as currently running (source hydrator piloted on a RollingSync ApplicationSet repo, each hydrator push restarting the wave), and it also forbids what T-24578 requests: Source Hydrator support for ApplicationSets to drive ordered multi-cluster deprovisioning. That request is scheduled as if the restriction did not exist; the note assigns the restriction to the pilot ticket but names no owner for the debounce work that lifts it.

The incident runbook rule to 'switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand' stands as long as T-28511's delete/recreate loop is open, and it directly forbids operating the PRD's flagship Reverse deletionOrder — which 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next', the exact wait T-28511 shows never completing on a stuck-Progressing child. The PRD's Risks section says 'No immediate Risks to consider' while its own strategy reproduced an infinite loop in staging.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', T-26443 documents stale-manifest syncs occurring precisely because 'the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests', and note-1 records that this promoter 'is still the shell script, nobody owns it' — parked. A cross-team dependency load-bearing for both the hydrator design and an open bug has no named owner.

T-28927 aims to promote Progressive Sync to Stable ('tested and validated... mature'), but the corpus shows the maturity precondition is not true yet: T-27949 leaves children OutOfSync on spec-only changes in v3.4.2, T-28511's delete/recreate loop has only an operational mitigation, and note-2's interim restrictions (AllAtOnce-before-manual-delete, no progressive sync on hydrator pilots) are still standing rules, not lifted.

RFC-002 resolves external Helm values by recommending 'the umbrella chart approach' since only one drySource is allowed, but T-24417 reports that switching to helm dependencies 'makes it difficult to use with ApplicationSets to control the chart version across environments' and asks for a Chart field on DrySource instead. The RFC's chosen simplification is the workflow a user workstream has already found unworkable, and no ticket reconciles the two.

Note-1 reprioritizes the dev pair from hydrator rollback (T-27327) onto 'the progressive sync deletion loop', while note-2 simultaneously restricts hydrator pilots from using progressive sync and restricts deletion ordering via the runbook. The same platform group is staffing the deletion workstream in the same period its own incident review constrained both halves of it — the schedule and the restrictions were set in separate meetings and neither document cites the other.

The platform sync call decided impersonation rolls out behind a per-project flag, but RFC-001's Goals state the feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' via applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation in argocd-cm, applicable to all Applications once flipped. The rollout decision assumes a per-project control surface the design does not provide, so the actual access change on enablement is fleet-wide, and any review process scoped per project is watching a control that does not exist.

The organization holds two incompatible accounts of which identity performs the diff under impersonation. Note-1 records the T-26271 root cause as 'diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch'; T-28695 demonstrates the opposite for the controller path: diff 'runs as the cluster credential from the cluster Secret' and ignores destinationServiceAccounts, while T-26271's own error names system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server. Until this is settled and recorded on the ticket, access reviews and audit-trail expectations are attached to the wrong acting identity, and the note itself admits the root cause was never written back to the ticket.

RFC-001's stated security outcome (least-privilege decoupling of sync from the control-plane credential) is silently undone by Server-Side Diff: because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, T-28695 shows the standing cluster credential must accumulate real, unbounded 'patch' write authority just to compute diffs, with safety resting on the dryRun=All convention rather than any enforced boundary. The narrow credential RFC-001 promises for control-plane operations is being progressively re-widened (five grant rounds so far) with no end state, and an auditor reviewing the cluster role sees write authority that no design document authorizes.

The strategy document commits that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and teardown 'remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time', while the Progressive Sync Deletion PRD ships exactly that mechanism as the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse). Note-2 records that someone spotted this disagreement in the incident review and it still has no owner; both commitments cannot hold.

The PRD's Security Considerations assert 'no additional roles or privileges are needed... no impact on the security aspects', but T-28511 shows the reverse/ordered deletion behavior already produced an infinite delete/re-create loop when a manually deleted Application is stuck Progressing, and the only mitigation is an operational rule ('switch to AllAtOnce before deleting any child app by hand') that lives solely in raw incident notes. A standing control that exists only in a personal note, not in the runbook artifact the ticket or PRD references, is a control an auditor cannot verify and a new operator will not find.

RFC-002 introduces a new privileged writer, the commit server acting via a repository-write secret (githubAppID/githubAppPrivateKey), and its own open question proposes branch protection 'only allow pushes to argo/* from the argo bot' as the control. T-28239 shows the integrity control does not follow this new identity: the hydrator pushes unsigned commits, so enabling signature verification on the hydrated branch makes Argo CD reject its own output, meaning the org currently cannot have both the bot-writer and commit-signature enforcement. The two documents describe the two halves of one governance gap without citing each other's control.

T-27327 proposes that rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' in both hydrator modes, while RFC-002's push-to-stage mode exists precisely so an external promotion system gates what reaches the deployment branch. If implemented, the hydrator's repository-write credential performs deploy-branch writes that skip the promotion control, and T-26443 already documents that push-to-stage plus auto-sync deploys whatever the branch last held. The audit story for 'every deployed change has a dry commit and passed promotion' breaks for rollbacks, and no document assigns who reviews these bypass writes.

T-27833 is an open access-control request that converges on RFC-001's impersonation model but demands a granularity the design explicitly rejects: the ticket wants namespace bootstrap done by the Argo CD control-plane SA while sync runs as an impersonated SA stripped of 'kind: namespace' permissions, whereas RFC-001 fixes the impersonated service account 'on a per Application level rather than on per resource level'. If impersonation ships as designed, this request is not satisfied, and the ticket's demonstrated boundary escape (committing a namespace manifest that overwrites managedNamespaceMetadata security labels) remains open; the pair needs an explicit disposition rather than an assumed fix.

RFC-001 mitigates privilege escalation 'by only allowing admin users to configure service account used for the sync operation at the AppProject level', while the strategy document's completed 'Project scoped repository and clusters' work deliberately moved project configuration toward self-service so 'end users can perform the change independently' instead of asking an administrator. As AppProject editing becomes self-service, the admin-only assumption underpinning the impersonation escalation control erodes: a tenant who can edit destinationServiceAccounts can select a more privileged SA, and RFC-001 itself allows mapping to cluster-admin-class accounts when AppProject config permits it. No document states who reviews destinationServiceAccounts changes under the self-service model.

RFC-002's commit server writes machine-generated commits into git, the organization's system of record, with a README 'Author' field templated from the human dry-commit author ({{ .commitAuthor }}), while T-28239 states those hydrated commits are pushed unsigned today, so when signature verification is enabled Argo CD rejects its own output. Together these show the hydrated branch contains machine acts attributed to a human's name with no cryptographic way to prove which is which until the opt-in commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits signing lands.

RFC-002 relies on a shared GitHub App credential (secret-type: repository-write, githubAppPrivateKey) for all hydrator pushes and says only that 'it's the application controller's job to ensure that the user has write access to the repo before making the call.' The access check is on the requesting user, but the commit of record is made by the org-wide App identity, and T-28239 proposes one cluster-wide signing key. Any tenant able to trigger hydration produces org-attributed, potentially org-signed commits, so authorship of a bad push cannot be traced to the individual actor from the record itself.

The strategy document commits that 'Deletion of generated Applications is explicitly out of scope... Teardown remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time,' while the PRD proposes automated ordered deletion via the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) on ApplicationSetStrategy. Both cannot hold; note-2 records that someone spotted the disagreement but 'not deciding here,' so the published commitment stands unamended while implementation proceeds against it.

The PRD asserts 'No immediate Risks to consider' and no security impact for automated deletion, but T-28511 documents an infinite delete/re-create loop under RollingSync with deletion ordering, and note-2's incident review makes an operator runbook (switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before manually deleting any child app) the standing control. Automation moved the deleting act from a human to the applicationset-controller, yet the only named holder of responsibility for safe deletion is an operator following an uncommitted runbook rule that appears in no ticket or spec.

Note-1 records a real decision that impersonation rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide,' but RFC-001's Goals state 'The feature can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications.' The decided rollout granularity is not something the specified mechanism (applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation in argocd-cm) can deliver, and the decision exists only in an unattributed meeting dump, not in the governing RFC.

RFC-001 answers its audit question by asserting Kubernetes audit trail events capture both the actual and impersonating user, but T-28695 shows the diff path ignores destinationServiceAccounts and runs server-side apply dry-runs as the standing cluster credential ('User "argocd"'), while sync runs as the impersonated SA. The same Application's actions therefore appear in the audit record under two different identities depending on code path, and the diff workaround requires granting real, unbounded patch authority to the cluster credential because RBAC has no dry-run verb — undermining the audit and least-privilege posture RFC-001 relies on.

Operative facts about live incidents are held only in anonymous notes rather than the records the organization relies on: note-1 states T-26271's root cause (with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account lacking patch on cluster-scoped resources) was established on a call but 'someone should note the root cause on that ticket,' and that T-27327's deprioritization 'should say so' on the ticket. Neither ticket carries these facts, so the systems of record misstate both the state of a security-relevant defect and the roadmap, and no author of the deciding record can be identified.

Provenance of the ticket corpus itself is asserted but not provable from the corpus: every ticket header claims 'verbatim base; see PROVENANCE.md for edits' (e.g. T-26271, T-9095), yet no PROVENANCE.md exists among the reviewed materials, so which passages are verbatim upstream text and which are local edits — and by whom — can only be assumed. If these records are relied on for engineering or compliance decisions, the missing edit record is a gap in authorship proof. Recommendation: the attribution, signed-commit, and audit-identity exposures above (org-attributed machine commits, cluster-wide signing key, dual-identity audit trails) should be routed to licensed counsel in the organization's operating jurisdiction before the hydrator push and signing features ship; this review drafts and issue-spots only and is not legal advice.

The strategy explicitly promises that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and teardown 'remains a manual operator action', while the PRD commits to shipping a 'deletionOrder' field with a 'Reverse' strategy that automates ordered deletion of ApplicationSet applications. Both cannot hold; the incident review note already flags that 'those two disagree, needs an owner', so the call is currently unowned.

RFC-001's stated goal is that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but the platform sync recorded a firm decision ('a real decision, not a maybe') that rollout goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. The spec as written cannot deliver the rollout the platform team committed to; RFC-001's approvers own reconciling the granularity.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section says 'No immediate Risks to consider', but field evidence shows the reverse deletion order (which 'waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next') already produced an infinite delete/re-create loop when a child app is stuck Progressing, reproduced in staging, with an incident runbook mandating a switch to AllAtOnce as mitigation. The plan's zero-risk assumption is contradicted by its own incident record.

RFC-002 declares 'Implementing a change promotion system' a non-goal, yet its push-to-stage mode depends on 'some external system to move changes to the deployment branch'. Field evidence shows that dependency failing: stale hydrated manifests get auto-synced 'only when the hydrator runs in push-to-stage mode; the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests', and the promoter is 'still the shell script, nobody owns it'. The product is shipping a mode whose correctness rests on an explicitly out-of-scope, unowned component.

RFC-002's core opinion is that 'every change to an application's desired state must originate from a commit to a single GitOps repository' via the dry source, and its push-to-stage design makes the staging branch the promotion integration point. The rollback proposal breaks both: it has rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' by checking out old rendered manifests rather than re-hydrating from a dry commit, producing deployed state with no originating dry commit. Note-1 records the rollback work deprioritized to next quarter, so the contradiction is unresolved, not decided.

T-26271 (CLI diff failing after 'we recently enabled the sync impersonation flag') and T-28695 (application-controller Server-Side Diff ignoring destinationServiceAccounts on external clusters) are the same underlying gap in RFC-001: the RFC decouples sync privileges via impersonation but never specifies which identity the diff path uses, so server-side apply dry-run authorizes as 'patch' under the wrong identity in both components. Note-1's root cause ('diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch') confirms the connection, yet T-28695 records maintainers scoping T-26271 away from external clusters instead of treating them as one spec defect.

T-24578 (Source Hydrator for ApplicationSets, motivated by 'control the destroy order of Application creation/deletion') and the PRD's deletionOrder proposal address the same user need — ordered teardown of ApplicationSet children — without citing each other. One routes it through hydrated app-of-apps sync waves, the other through a rollingSync-coupled deletionOrder field; shipping both creates two incompatible answers to one promise, and neither document decides which is the product's path.

The hydrator pilot and progressive sync collide mechanically: the incident review confirmed 'each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave' and ruled that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, yet T-27949 describes exactly that combination live ('we are also piloting the source hydrator on this repository... each of those commits is picked up as a source change'). The restriction was never written onto the pilot ticket, so the next team will re-trip the known failure.

T-28927 proposes promoting Progressive Sync to Stable, defined as 'tested and validated with various use cases', but the data to know it works does not exist: T-27846 states 'getting a wide-eye view of progressive sync is difficult' and the metrics to answer basic questions (did the wave start, which app is it waiting for) are still only a proposal, while T-27949 shows even the failure case left no evidence ('logs were at warn level, so no relevant progressive-sync transition logs were emitted'). The success measure for Stable cannot currently be evaluated.

T-27833's proposed solution requires splitting resource handling between the control plane and the impersonated SA per resource kind ('which resources are handled by the Argo CD control plane and which... by the impersonated SA'), but RFC-001 already answered this shape of request in the negative: 'The service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level.' The ticket is relying on a capability the spec explicitly rules out; RFC-001's approvers own whether to relax the per-Application constraint.

Progressive Sync is being scoped for promotion to Stable while the observability needed to validate that maturity is still an open request: T-27846 asks for the basic metrics (time to trigger, time per step, refreshes caused by the ApplicationSet, why a sync is not starting) and none exist yet, so 'tested and validated with various use cases' cannot be demonstrated with production numbers. The promotion ticket does not name the metrics ticket as a dependency.

The RollingSync failure in T-27949 was unobservable when it happened: the report explicitly notes the ApplicationSet controller logs were at warn level so no progressive-sync transition logs were emitted, and the rollout reported complete while children were OutOfSync. Question 4 of T-27846 ('My sync is not starting, why/which Applications is it waiting for?') is precisely the missing instrumentation; until it lands, this failure mode is only detectable by manually comparing child status.sync.status against ApplicationSet status.applicationStatus.

Note-2's confirmed mechanism that every hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave has no measurement: T-27846's requested metric 'How much Application refresh were caused by the ApplicationSet' is exactly the number that would move, and it is not recorded anywhere. The interim rule (hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists) therefore has no observable exit criterion — nobody can measure whether a future debounce reduced wave restarts because there is no before baseline.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section states 'No immediate Risks to consider', but the Reverse strategy's own mechanism — 'Waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next application' — is exactly the wait that T-28511 shows never completing when a child app is stuck Progressing, producing an infinite delete/re-create loop that note-2 says reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. Both cannot hold: a risk already observed in staging is not 'no immediate risks'.

The incident runbook mitigation in note-2 (switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting a child app) is unverified against the primary evidence: T-28511's own reproduction manifest already specifies 'deletionOrder: AllAtOnce' under the RollingSync strategy and still exhibits the Deleting/Syncing flip loop. The standing operational practice rests on an untested assumption, and no measurement (e.g. loop recurrence count under each deletionOrder) exists to confirm the mitigation works.

The strategy roadmap commits that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and teardown 'remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time', while the PRD proposes shipping exactly that as the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse, maybe Custom) on ApplicationSetStrategy. Note-2 records that this disagreement was noticed but deliberately left unowned ('needs an owner. not deciding here').

T-26271's reporter is still chasing the wrong cause in the ticket text ('the cluster Secret credential itself is broad, so we don't understand why the diff suddenly runs with a narrower identity'), while note-1 records the root cause was already found on the platform sync call: with impersonation on, the diff runs as the destination service account lacking patch on cluster-scoped resources. The correction was never written back to the ticket, so the organization's tracker and its actual knowledge diverge on the same defect.

Note-1's gating rule 'nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed' has no defined observable fix condition: T-28695 shows the diff path ignoring destinationServiceAccounts is structural (RBAC has no dry-run verb, so Server-Side Diff requires real patch authority, escalated five times with 'no end state'), and it is the only document carrying any measured baseline — client-side diff cost 'zero' across ~20 charts. Whether the per-project impersonation flag can ever go fleet-wide depends on resolving T-28695, and nothing in the corpus records that dependency or a metric (ComparisonError rate, Synced↔Unknown flips) that would signal the fix landed.

Note-1 deprioritizes hydrator rollback (T-27327) to next quarter while note-2 keeps the hydrator pilot (T-27949's repository) running; combined, pilot repos deploy from hydrated branches with no rollback path in the History & Rollback tab, which T-27327 identifies as the first question new onboarding users ask. If a pilot app needs an emergency rollback right now, the only path is a manual git operation, and no ticket records that exposure or measures how often pilots roll back.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', T-26443 shows that reliance already failing observably (auto-sync deploys stale manifests from the stage branch when the promoter has not yet moved fresh ones), and note-1 records that this external system 'is still the shell script, nobody owns it' — parked, not tracked. The promotion path every hydrator deployment depends on is unowned, unmonitored, and already implicated in a stale-sync failure mode.

T-27875's trigger condition — a new commit arriving while an app is still syncing to a previous commit, leaving it OutOfSync indefinitely without selfHeal — is exactly the traffic pattern RFC-002's hydrator manufactures: each dry commit produces machine-generated commits to the syncSource targetBranch that Argo CD then syncs, so hydrator adoption raises the frequency of the commit-during-sync race. Neither document cites the other, and the only current signal of the failure is a controller log line ('Skipping auto-sync: most recent sync already to'), not any metric.

T-27833's proposed mechanism (split which resources the control-plane SA handles versus the impersonated SA, so the impersonated SA can be denied kind: Namespace) contradicts a decision RFC-001 already recorded: impersonation is determined 'on a per Application level rather than on per resource level', and the feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level'. The ticket is effectively requesting a design the RFC's answered Open Questions rule out, without either document acknowledging the other.

T-26271's CI diff failures ('argocd-server is attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held', appearing only after 'we recently enabled the sync impersonation flag') are the direct consequence of RFC-001's impersonation design: once application.sync.impersonation.enabled is on, operations run as the AppProject's defaultServiceAccount rather than the broad cluster Secret credential, which is why the diff suddenly runs with a narrower identity. Note-1 records this exact root cause from the platform sync call but the ticket itself never mentions it.

T-28695's symptom (sync honors destinationServiceAccounts, Server-Side Diff runs as the raw cluster credential, forcing unbounded patch grants) traces to a scoping decision written into RFC-001: its Implementation Details fix only the sync path (Application Controller sync.go setting Impersonate config on the SyncContext), so the diff/reconcile path was never included in the impersonation design. The design does not acknowledge that its 'least privilege' goal is defeated on any cluster where Server-Side Diff is enabled.

T-26443's stale-manifest auto-sync symptom occurs, by the reporter's own observation, only in push-to-stage mode — which is exactly the gap RFC-002 designed in: push-to-stage 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch', with a promotion system explicitly a Non-Goal. The RFC never addresses what auto-sync does when syncSource.targetBranch changes while the external promoter lags; note-1's parked item that the stage-branch promoter 'is still the shell script, nobody owns it' is the same unowned seam.

T-27949's progressive-sync miss is aggravated by an RFC-002 design property the ticket only mentions in passing: the hydrator lands 'a fresh commit on the hydrated branch' every hydration cycle, and each commit is picked up as a source change. Note-2's incident review confirmed 'each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave' and imposed the interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync — a restriction neither RFC-002 nor the progressive-sync PRD acknowledges.

The strategy roadmap commits that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and teardown 'remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time', while the PRD proposes exactly that automated ordered teardown via the deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) in ApplicationSetStrategy. Note-2 flags the disagreement as needing an owner; neither document cites the other.

T-28511's delete/recreate infinite loop names the mechanism the PRD designed: the reverse deletion strategy 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving to the next', and a resource stuck in Progressing means that wait never completes, restarting the wave. The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section says 'No immediate Risks to consider' even though this symptom (with note-2's staging reproduction and the AllAtOnce-before-manual-delete runbook mitigation) is already filed against the design's core wait semantics.

RFC-001 states as a Goal that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but note-1 records the operational decision that the rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide' — a granularity the design as written does not support, so either the decision or the design must change.

T-24417's inability to point drySource at a Helm repository chart is a consequence of RFC-002's stated opinion, not an oversight: the RFC declares 'only one source may be used in as the dry source' (drySource carries only repoURL, targetRevision, path — no chart), rejects the multi-source pattern as nondeterministic, and directs users to the umbrella-chart approach — exactly the helm-dependencies workaround the ticket says makes ApplicationSet-based version control difficult.

T-27833's proposal (namespace bootstrap by the control-plane SA, everything else by the impersonated SA with kind: Namespace removed) collides with an explicit RFC-001 decision: the impersonation service account is determined 'on a per Application level rather than on per resource level', so the per-resource split of privileges the ticket asks for is precluded by the design as answered in the RFC's Open Questions.

T-24578's request for hydrator support in ApplicationSets to control destroy order and the PRD's deletionOrder field address the same underlying need — ordered teardown of ApplicationSet-generated Applications in multi-cluster deprovisioning — without citing each other: the PRD's Reverse strategy would remove the ticket's motivation for the app-of-apps sync-wave workaround for the single-ApplicationSet case, though the ticket's cross-ApplicationSet DAG ordering remains outside the PRD's scope.
